title: Remark
body_md: There are a few generalizations of ASMs to rectangular shape in the literature. We want to compare these notions to ASRs. The term \emph{partial ASMs} was coined by Heuer and Striker \cite{HS22} and it essentially denotes topleft corners of ASMs. These matrices had previously been introduced simply as ASMs by Behrend \cite{Beh08} and independently up to a horizontal reflection as \emph{alternating matrices} by Fortin \cite{For08}. ASRs are a proper subset of partial ASMs since nonempty rows have to sum to $1$. In joint work with Billey \cite{BK26}, the second author introduced \emph{quilts of alternating sign matrices}. In that context, quilts of type~$(C_r,C_k)$ are called rectangular ASMs of size $r \times k$. If $r \le k$, these rectangular ASMs are in bijective correspondence with \emph{monotone triangles} with $r$ rows and positive entries less than or equal to $k$ as defined by Fischer \cite{Fis06}, and correspond to row-complete ASRs in our terminology.

label: thm:Schroeder_ballot

title: Proof
body_md:
It is easy to see that $\mathrm{Sch}_{n,0}=1$, $\mathrm{Sch}_{n,n}=\mathrm{Sch}_{n}$ and $\mathrm{Sch}_{n,m}=\mathrm{Sch}_{n,m-1}+\mathrm{Sch}_{n-1,m}+\mathrm{Sch}_{n-1,m-1}$ for $n \ge m$ since $\mathrm{Sch}_{n-1,m}=0$ if $m=n$.

We show that the numbers $f(r,k) \coloneqq S^{312}_{{r},{k},{r}}-S^{312}_{{r},{k-1},{r}}$ fulfil the same recursion. It follows from \cref{thm:r=d} that $f(r,k)                                       
= \sum_{j=2}^r a_{r-1,j}\binom{k-r+j-1}{j-1}$ if $r \ge 2$.

For the initial conditions, we can easily see that $f(1,k)=1$ and $f(r,r)=\sum_{j=2}^{r} a_{r-1,j} = \mathrm{Sch}_{r-1}$. For the recursion relation, we consider the set of all Schr\"oder paths from $(0,0)$ to $(r-1,r-1)$, which we uniquely partition into segments such that each segment touches the diagonal exactly twice. If $j$ is the number of times the Schr\"oder path touches the diagonal, then we have $j-1$ segments. For a given $k \ge r$, we then label each segment by an integer from $1$ to $k-r+j-1$ such that the labels strictly increase from the start point to the end point of the Schr\"oder path. These labelled paths are enumerated by $f(r,k)$. With this combinatorial interpretation in mind, we prove that $f(r,k)=f(r,k-1)+f(r-1,k)+f(r-1,k-1)$. We partition our labelled Schr\"oder paths as follows: If none of the segments has the highest possible label $k-r+j-1$, then these paths are enumerated by $f(r,k-1)$. Note that this set of paths is empty if $k=r$, matching $f(r,r-1)=0$. Now assume that the last segment is decorated by the highest possible label $k-r+j-1$. If this segment consists of a simple diagonal step $(1,1)$, we remove this step to obtain a Schr\"oder path from $(0,0)$ to $(r-2,r-2)$ whose segments are increasingly labelled with integers from $\{1,\dots,k-r+j-2\}$; these paths are enumerated by $f(r-1,k-1)$. If the last segment of the path is not $(1,1)$, then it starts with a horizontal unit step and ends with a vertical unit step. We remove these two steps from the last segment and, provided that the remaining part is not empty, add the rest back again. Thus, we add new segments to the path, say $t$, to which we assign the consecutive labels $k-r+j,\dots,k-r+j+t-1$. The labelled Schr\"oder path has now $j+t-2$ segments. With the maximal label being $k-r+j+t-1 = k-(r-1)+(j+t-2)$ we obtain a class of labelled Schr\"oder paths enumerated by $f(r-1,k)$.
This proves $f(r,k)=f(r,k-1)+f(r-1,k)+f(r-1,k-1)$.
